implementation_notes: Go's compiler inlines aggressively and automatically, and it is the one mainstream language where you do not write an inline hint at all - there is no keyword. What Go gives instead is an explicit cost budget: the inliner refuses a function whose 'cost' (an AST-node count, 80 by default for the mid-stack inliner) exceeds the budget, and you can see it with -gcflags='-m'. That is why a long chain of small methods is fine in Go and a large one is not inlined, and why Go's advice is 'write small functions and let the compiler inline them' rather than 'mark functions for inlining'. Inlining is also the mechanism behind Go's zero-cost abstraction claim: an interface call is the case where inlining fails (the dynamic type is unknown), so interfaces in a hot path cost and concrete calls do not.
idiom_name: automatic inlining under the mid-stack cost budget (-gcflags='-m' to see decisions); no inline keyword exists
pitfalls: There is no inline keyword in Go: to 'force' inlining you restructure the function to be smaller, not to annotate it.
The cost budget is an AST-node count, so a function can fail to inline because of a syntactic detail (a defer, a range over a map) rather than its computational cost.
Interfaces are the inlining barrier: an interface call cannot be inlined because the dynamic type is unknown, so a hot path over an interface costs even when the concrete type is small.
Inlining decisions differ between the compiler's mid-stack and leaf inliners, so a function may inline into some callers and not others - which is why the -m output matters.
Measure on a release build; the debug build's line tables disable most inlining.
